Series::polygamma¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::polygamma(std::int64_t n) const
Series& Series::polygamma_(std::int64_t n)

What It Does¶

Computes the polygamma function of order n elementwise. Polygamma is the n-th derivative of the digamma function, equivalently the (n + 1)-th derivative of ln Gamma:

polygamma(n, x) = d^n/dx^n psi(x) = d^(n+1)/dx^(n+1) ln( Gamma(x) )

The low orders have their own names:

  • polygamma(0, x) is digamma(x).

  • polygamma(1, x) is the trigamma function — the one that appears as the gradient of digamma, and as the Fisher information of several one-parameter families.

  • polygamma(2, x) is tetragamma, and so on.

For n >= 1 the closed form is a Hurwitz zeta value:

polygamma(n, x) = (-1)^(n+1) * n! * zeta(n + 1, x)

so polygamma alternates in sign with n: order 1 is positive, order 2 is negative, order 3 positive. The forward pass uses that identity with an Euler-Maclaurin evaluation of zeta, accurate to full precision in a handful of terms.

Anchor facts:

  • polygamma(1, 1) = pi^2 / 6 = 1.6449341.

  • polygamma(1, x + 1) = polygamma(1, x) - 1/x^2, the derivative of the digamma recurrence.

  • polygamma(2, 1) = -2 * zeta(3) = -2.4041138.

  • Every order has poles at 0 and the negative integers. For n >= 1, the implementation follows the Hurwitz-zeta continuation used by the established tensor convention: those poles are represented by signed infinity, while negative non-integers can have finite values.

polygamma() is out-of-place; polygamma_() overwrites the current storage.

Parameters¶

n (std::int64_t): derivative order. Must be >= 0. n = 0 routes to digamma.

Returns¶

Series or Series& A Series with the same shape as self, each element replaced by polygamma(n, x). polygamma_() returns a reference to the mutated series.

An integral input is promoted to float64; floating-point input keeps its dtype. The in-place form requires floating-point storage.

Gradient¶

polygamma(n, .) is differentiable with respect to x. Its derivative is the next order:

d/dx polygamma(n, x) = polygamma(n + 1, x)

The backward pass evaluates that higher order the same way the forward pass does. n is a structural integer argument and carries no gradient. At a pole, the value or sensitivity can be infinite; near a pole, expect very large magnitudes.

Examples¶

Example 1. Order 0 is digamma.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}).polygamma(0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.5772, 0.4228, 0.9228]

Example 2. Order 1 is trigamma. At x = 1 the value is pi^2 / 6.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}).polygamma(1));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.6449, 0.6449, 0.3949]

Successive entries drop by 1/x^2: 1.6449341 - 1 = 0.6449341, then 0.6449341 - 1/4 = 0.3949341.

Example 3. Order 2 at x = 1 is -2 * zeta(3).

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0}).polygamma(2));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-2.4041, -0.4041]

Example 4. Negative non-integers are not rejected. Their value follows the same continuation identity; here the trigamma recurrence crosses the pole at zero.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-0.5, 0.5, 1.5}).polygamma(1));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[8.9348, 4.9348, 0.9348]

Example 5. The backward pass of order n is order n + 1.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.5, 2.5});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.polygamma(1).sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());
pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({1.5, 2.5}).polygamma(2));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.8288, -0.2362]
Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.8288, -0.2362]

Example 6. Poles at 0 and the negative integers diverge.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.0, -1.0, 2.0}).polygamma(1));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[inf, inf, 0.6449]

Example 7. A negative order is rejected.

try {
  std::cout << pluss::make_series({1.0}).polygamma(-1);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

polygamma: n must be >= 0

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • n must be >= 0. A negative order raises polygamma: n must be >= 0.

  • n = 0 is digamma, not a constant; do not expect polygamma(0, x) to be 1.

  • For n >= 1 the sign alternates: odd orders are positive on the positive axis, even orders negative (the (-1)^(n+1) factor). n = 0 (digamma) is not sign-definite.

  • Poles at 0 and the negative integers diverge. Negative non-integers are valid continuation points and can return finite values.

  • Integral input promotes out of place, but polygamma_() requires a floating-point receiver.

  • n carries no gradient; only x does.

Summary¶

polygamma(n, x) is the n-th derivative of digamma:

  • polygamma(0, .) is digamma; polygamma(1, .) is trigamma

  • for n >= 1, equals (-1)^(n+1) * n! * zeta(n + 1, x)

  • sign alternates with n on the positive axis; poles diverge, while negative non-integers are continued

  • differentiable in x with backward polygamma(n + 1, x); n is structural

  • polygamma_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::digamma: the n = 0 case and the function polygamma differentiates.

  • Series::zeta: the Hurwitz zeta the closed form is built from.

  • Series::lgamma: polygamma(n, .) is its (n + 1)-th derivative.
